title: Run Untrusted Agent Code with LangSmith Sandboxes | Interrupt 26

segments.text: Hi everyone.
I lead our infrastructure team and I'm super excited to talk about running untrusted agent code
with LangSmith Sandboxes.
Usually they don't let the infrastructure team outside the basement, so I'm super excited
to be here today.
I think if you look across the last six months, one thing that we're seeing as a transitionary
point across the industry is that agents are writing real code today.
Quick show of hands — who here uses Claude Code, Devin,
the agent CLI, et cetera?
Yeah, pretty packed house — I'd guess maybe like 70%
of the people in here raised their hand on using coding agents.
Sundar Pichai recently said 75% of code at Google
is being generated by AI.
GitHub released a lot of statistics
around the PR and code percentages that they're seeing.
41% of commits this year seem to be coming from AI as well.
Stripe published a blog where 1,300 PRs per week
are just generated by their internal Minions coding agent.
So we're seeing coding agents as this mega-shift
that's here to stay.
The first main use case that we've seen
is in the field of software engineering,
which is probably what brings most of you here.
OpenSWE is our internal open source coding agent
that we use as well.
It's connected to our Slack, GitHub, et cetera.
And it commits hundreds of PRs across our variety of repos.
Claude Code needs no introduction.
Basically, it's taking Anthropic to the moon.
Devin is doing tons of cool stuff with sandboxing as well,
with local coding and being able to hand it off to the cloud.
And Ramp's written a lot of blogs about their Insights agent
and how they've built this validation loop where
you can take screenshots and convert things to code completely
autonomously, and keep humans just doing the management part.
But actually, we're seeing this expand to tons of other use
cases as well.
It turns out that giving an agent access to a computer
is actually super powerful.
Data analysis is a big emerging trend as well.
Instead of providing predefined SQL tools and things like that,
you might just give your agent the ability to write scripts
and load data as a CSV.
And it can figure out how to generate a graph
or do analysis as well.
So we're seeing this in the financial space with companies
like Julius.
We see it in data analysis products like Hex.
So a very, very popular trend as well
that we're seeing is this extension of coding
agents.
Security — another super interesting one.
Companies like Xbow, Koridor, et cetera,
will run automated pen tests against your infrastructure.
So you tell an agent to try and figure out what's wrong.
And they'll autonomously run
and perform really powerful penetration testing
that typically would be super labor-intensive.
And this is kind of an extension of the ability
to execute code — this idea of browser
and computer use, right?
So not only are we allowing the agent to write code,
we're allowing it to actually control a browser
or control your entire system.
Some examples of this would be Stagehand,
which does automated Playwright testing.
You can have it non-deterministically
go through your UI and verify bugs.
Claude's computer use can control your whole system
and do cool things there as well.
But as Uncle Ben once said
in Spider-Man: with great power comes great responsibility.
It's actually super risky to just allow
an untrusted thing to execute code randomly.
These are all from this year.
Earlier this year — well, actually last month —
we had the "sci-holude" supply chain attack.
That would basically, if you installed the package,
just export all credentials that were on your machine.
We don't even really trust humans to deal with this —
I don't necessarily trust an agent to do that either.
Top tech startups are even running into
issues like this, where n8n recently
had a sandbox escape vulnerability
where you could use certain JavaScript tricks
to escape the sandbox that they provided.
And prompt injection is a concern for anyone building
agentic apps.
Recently, Google's AI agent browser
had an issue where you could inject into the prompt to actually
escape their sandbox environment.
And that's where this idea of a sandbox comes in.
It's this separate infrastructure primitive that
allows you to execute code safely and remove it
from your core runtime.
There are a couple of key characteristics of this.
There are also different levels of sandboxing,
where you might be sandboxing just code execution,
or you might be sandboxing an entire computer, et cetera.
But that's what the core primitive is.
And that's also where LangSmith Sandboxes comes in,
because building this primitive is actually quite hard
for a number of reasons that I'll walk through.
The first problem is that agents are becoming user-facing.
So users expect faster responses.
I get pretty mad if I'm waiting a few seconds
for a response.
I think we've gotten a little OK with it for LLM apps,
because LLMs take a while to respond.
But you still want near real-time latencies.
And user-facing workloads are also fairly dynamic
and can scale up to thousands.
You might have bursty workloads, things like that.
With LangSmith Sandboxes, we solved this
with the ability to scale.
We're actually a little bit faster than this —
we constantly benchmark this
and are constantly working to speed up our sandbox spin-up
time.
But we have a P50 of 0.98 seconds right now.
So, a little update here.
You can also spin up thousands of sandboxes dynamically.
So you don't need to maintain the compute
to run thousands of these things.
We'll do that for you and make sure
it's orchestrated and cached well.
The other problem is that with users
you also get bad actors — people who
are trying to leverage your compute and do bad things with it.
Container escapes are a huge problem that we've seen,
and kind of show that containers alone are not
enough for this kind of product.
Just recently, there was a container escape attack
where you could have a 700-byte script
and get access to the full host kernel
and do malicious things to your environment.
Prompt injection — I already mentioned — a poisoned README or something can get your agent to
just export the environment to a random website, and things like that.
Malicious MCP servers are also just another area that we're seeing used as a honeypot to get
your agents to do bad things.
On the LangSmith Sandboxes side, we have this concept of an auth proxy.
Basically, all network traffic goes through the sandbox.
And so you can lock down the environment — kind of how you would a computer
in an enterprise.
You can set allowlists, denylists, keep credentials as part of the proxy,
so there's nothing sensitive in the runtime itself.
And this is super powerful.
You can block malicious MCPs — even if you get prompt injected, you can survive.
And we're really excited about this as a core primitive part of our sandboxes.
The third problem is that agents are long-running and interruptible, and we're
only seeing these get longer and longer running.
Sandboxes need to be able to start on demand, pause, and resume.
And you also don't want to lose that state.
If I turn off my local computer and turn it back on,
I have all my files still there.
The agent expects that same thing as well.
And that's super powerful.
Traditional workloads don't really support that.
So with LangSmith Sandboxes, we've enabled this
with a durable persistence layer.
So any state that you build up on your machine, you can keep.
You can also throw it away if you want.
We support the ability to pause and resume.
Because we have super fast spin-up,
you can spin it down during inactivity
and spin it back up — only paying for the compute
you're actually using.
We also have no limits on how long
you can keep a sandbox alive.
Most other providers have a limit —
you can keep it up for four hours or something like that.
We have no limits, because we know that maybe you want
your agent to just be running in the background for hours
or even days.
And then we also have the ability to have multiple agents
interacting with the sandbox.
So if you have shared state
that you want multiple agents to work on —
just like your local computer —
you can do that as well.
And the last problem that we're seeing
is that agents make mistakes.
Most of you are probably doing evals
to try and prevent a lot of this,
but agents can always make mistakes.
And this is just a problem inherent
to the stochasticity of these things.
So on the sandbox side,
we support a bunch of capabilities that help with this.
At any given time, you can snapshot.
And what that really empowers is the ability
to also restore.
So I recently had an agent delete my /etc/resolv.conf —
broke all DNS.
I wish I could have checkpointed and restored,
but unfortunately I didn't have that.
But you can do this in our cloud.
You can also fork.
So take that initial state and maybe try out
10 different things if you want to continue
from that point.
You can get started with one line of code today.
It's part of our LangSmith SDKs, so feel free to get started.
It's available on all paid plans, as I mentioned.
You can bring your own filesystem.
So if you already have Docker images
that you might be building, et cetera,
with packages that you want installed, or a CLI,
whatever — that works out of the box.
And it plugs into your stack.
This wouldn't be LangChain if we didn't have a rich open source
ecosystem around our products.
You can use this with LangGraph agents, OpenAI
SDK — we have a CLI, tons of features across the board in our open source as well.
We have a lot on our roadmap.
We're very early in the lifecycle of this product.
I was mentioning local-remote handoff, which I'm super excited about.
Shared volumes is another one.
So bring the same code or files to a bunch of different agents at the same time.
And then — we're an observability company —
we also want to support full execution tracing.
So you can see what's actually happening on your sandbox as well.
Try it on LangSmith today.
It's available on all paid plans,
released in all our SDKs,
and we'd love to hear your feedback.
Thank you — my name is Mikhail.
(audience applauding)
I do have to say, it takes a village —
our whole team has been working on this,
so very thankful for them.
I'll be around all day, so if you're excited about this,
please come chat.
